title: The Bell of Old Chapel Road
premise: Hospice nurse Rosalind Eastwick has always heard the dying count backwards, a private curse she manages with rituals of light and locked doors. When the church bell of Hollowmere — melted down in 1911 — begins to ring at dusk, the whole village falls under its pull, drawn toward Old Chapel Road to sing a verse no one remembers learning. Rosalind discovers the bell demands a final verse completed by a living voice, and that her own blood helped cast it; her great-grandmother's name is scored inside the bronze. To save the village she must learn the song's last verse without ever singing along, trading her voice, her love for the village doctor, and finally her place among the living — ending with Rosalind becoming the bell's new keeper, ringing only for the dying, counting them gently home.
about_author: Coral Eastwick is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent eleven years in palliative wards across northern England before turning to writing. She lives near the coast with too many clocks, all of which she keeps deliberately unsynchronized.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. On her hospice rounds, Mr. Tallow counts backwards from thirty and dies exactly at one, as they all do. Rosalind performs her rituals: lights on, doors counted twice. The beat is weary competence masking dread, establishing her curse and her rules.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A quiet domestic chapter showing her rituals in full: salted thresholds, every bulb burning, the notebook of names who died at one. Dr. Elias Marsh notices her exhaustion and offers kindness she deflects. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for control.

chapters.title: A Bell That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At dusk, a deep bell tolls over Hollowmere. The parish records say the bell was melted down in 1911. Only Rosalind seems to hear it clearly; others feel a vague homesickness pulling eastward. Beat: first crack in her ordered world.

chapters.title: Old Chapel Road
chapters.summary: Rosalind follows the sound to the roofless chapel ruins where no bell hangs, yet the air shudders with each toll. She finds fresh-worn footprints leading in, none leading out. Beat: dread sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: The Verse No One Taught Us
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Villagers hum fragments of an unfamiliar hymn at odd hours — the baker mid-loaf, children skipping rope. Rosalind realizes the song is spreading. Beat: contagion of the mind, community beginning to slip.

chapters.title: Elias Asks Questions
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The doctor interviews the humming patients and finds their memories rewritten around the melody. He turns to Rosalind, the only immune-seeming person he knows. Beat: alliance forming, tenderness flickering under professional concern.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A dying woman grabs Rosalind's wrist and sings three lines of the verse perfectly, then says: 'Your family poured it.' Rosalind searches parish archives that night. Beat: personal stakes detonate — this is inheritance, not accident.

chapters.title: The Eastwick Ledger
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In the archive she finds an 1911 foundry ledger: the old bell was recast with 'a tithe of voices' — thirteen villagers entombed in the bronze, among them an Eastwick. Beat: horror of lineage; guilt arrives generations late.

chapters.title: First Missing
chapters.summary: Constable Dyer's POV. The verger vanishes; his boots stand neatly at the chapel ruin facing the empty tower. Search parties form. Beat: the village's denial curdling into fear.

chapters.title: The Pull
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Walking home, her own feet drift toward Old Chapel Road; she wakes with mud to her knees and the verse two lines richer in her head. Beat: the horror is inside her now, growing without consent.

chapters.title: Salt and Iron
chapters.summary: Rosalind and Elias's shared POV. They attempt folk protections — iron nails, salt circles, wax in the ears. Nothing holds past dusk. Elias admits he hears it too, faintly. Beat: intimacy through shared helplessness; rules failing.

chapters.title: The Choir at Midnight
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She witnesses the vanished villagers standing in the ruin, singing in unison, faces serene and wrong, mouths moving slightly out of sync with the sound. Beat: body-horror of harmony; they are instruments now.

chapters.title: Mother Bell
chapters.summary: Archive interlude, 1911 letters read aloud in Rosalind's POV. The foundry master's daughter describes the casting: the bell 'drinks the verse' and must be fed its last line by a free voice or it takes the town entire. Beat: the mechanism revealed — and the deadline implied.

chapters.title: One Hundred and Eleven Days
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Cross-referencing disappearances with lunar and liturgical dates, Elias calculates the bell completes its feeding at the winter solstice. Six weeks out. Beat: clock starts ticking; hope and doom in equal measure.

chapters.title: The Humming Child
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Little Wren Ashcombe hums the verse flawlessly and doesn't remember her mother's face. Rosalind shields the girl, hardening her resolve. Beat: protective love as fuel; innocence as collateral.

chapters.title: Doors That Won't Lock
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Her rituals fail one by one — doors swing open, lights gutter at dusk precisely. The house itself seems to lean toward the road. Beat: sanctuary revoked; nowhere left that isn't the bell's.

chapters.title: The Second Missing
chapters.summary: Dyer's POV. Three more vanish overnight, including the constable's own deputy. The village splits: some want to burn the chapel ruins, others have begun walking there voluntarily at dusk. Beat: social fracture; the bell weaponizes belonging.

chapters.title: Fire Against Bronze
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The burning party reaches the ruin and the bell tolls once — everyone within earshot kneels involuntarily. The fire dies in wet air. Beat: futility of force; power displayed casually, corruptingly.

chapters.title: What It Offers
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In a dream the bell speaks with her great-grandmother's voice: finish the verse willingly and rule the song — choose who lives, who rings, who rests. Power offered like a hand. Beat: temptation; corruption's gentle opening bid.

chapters.title: Elias's Bargain
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Desperate to protect Rosalind, Elias secretly approaches the ruin offering himself. The bell refuses him — his voice is 'not of the line.' He hides this from her. Beat: love against duty, secrets as rot.

chapters.title: Wren's Drawing
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Wren draws the chapel interior from memory: thirteen figures in the walls, and a fourteenth figure holding a small hammer — a figure with Rosalind's face. Beat: prophecy via child's eye; destiny closing like a door.

chapters.title: The Foundry Book's Last Page
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The ledger's torn final page surfaces in Tallow's effects: instructions for 'unringing' — the last verse sung backwards by a blood heir who never joins the song aloud. One mistake and she joins the bronze. Beat: the plan exists, razor-thin.

chapters.title: Learning Backwards
chapters.summary: Rosalind and Elias's POV. Rosalind practices the reversed verse silently, mouthing shapes, writing it in mirror-script so she never speaks it forward. Elias coaches her like a singer protecting a fragile instrument. Beat: tender discipline; love expressed as rehearsal.

chapters.title: The Toll Takes Tallow's Sister
chapters.summary: Village POV. Edith Tallow walks into the dusk choir smiling, waving goodbye. The town stops pretending. Rosalind's guilt peaks — she could end this and hasn't yet dared. Beat: cost of hesitation made flesh.

chapters.title: Quarantine of Song
chapters.summary: Elias and Dyer's POV. They seal the eastern road, plug ears with wax, post watchers. The bell simply rings lower, felt in the chest rather than heard, and the watchers begin swaying. Beat: containment fails; the bell adapts.

chapters.title: Rosalind Sings (Almost)
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Half-asleep, she catches herself humming the verse forward and stops at the penultimate note, tasting bronze. Something in her chest 'sets' like cooling metal. Beat: near-catastrophe; the stakes are now anatomical.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Confession
chapters.summary: Dream sequence, Rosalind's POV. Her great-grandmother appears not as tempter but prisoner: she tried to unring the bell in 1912 and failed halfway; her voice has been ringing ever since. She teaches Rosalind the true final line. Beat: inherited failure met with inherited courage.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The village prepares unknowingly for the end — suppers, candles, children bedded down. Elias and Rosalind admit their love plainly, knowing what tomorrow costs. Beat: stillness before the storm; love stated without future tense.

chapters.title: The Longest Night Begins
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At sundown the bell rings continuously. Choir-villagers converge on the ruin singing the verse forward, needing one free voice to complete it. Rosalind walks up Old Chapel Road by choice. Beat: duty embraced; terror walked through.

chapters.title: Thirteen Voices
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Inside the ruin she sees the taken villagers suspended in the bell's resonance, including Edith and the verger, eyes pleading. The bell offers her power one final time: rule instead of release. Beat: climax of temptation; she refuses aloud — nearly fatal.

chapters.title: The Reversed Verse
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She sings the verse backwards, each syllable costing warmth and color; frost climbs her arms, her reflection grays. The bell's toll bends, cracks, descends through impossible registers. Beat: climax; sacrifice rendered physically, line by line.

chapters.title: One Mistake
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. On the final line her voice breaks — she slips one note forward. The bell surges; Elias throws himself between her and the sound, singing the corrected note with his mortal, off-key voice. Beat: love against duty consummated in error and repair.

chapters.title: Unringing
chapters.summary: Shared POV. The bell falls silent mid-toll for the first time since 1911. The bronze cools and splits along a hairline seam. Thirteen figures collapse onto the frost, breathing, weeping, alive but marked. Beat: release; the exhale after drowning.

chapters.title: The Price
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Rosalind survives but her voice is gone above a whisper, and she can no longer hear the dying count — she hears nothing at all, a silence she must relearn to live inside. Beat: survival's invoice; grief and gratitude tangled.

chapters.title: Aftermath in Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Winter passes. The returned remember everything and mostly forgive themselves; the village quietly dismantles the chapel stones and builds a low garden wall instead. Beat: communal healing, imperfect and unsentimental.

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Wren asks whether the bell is really gone. Rosalind writes her answer: bells don't die, they wait. That night, far off, a single soft toll — different, smaller, almost kind. Beat: ambiguity restored; peace with an asterisk.

chapters.title: The New Keeper
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind understands the silence in her wasn't emptiness but vacancy: she is the keeper now, bound to ring for the dying so they needn't count alone. She accepts it as vocation, not curse. Beat: theme resolved — the price of survival becomes a chosen service.

chapters.title: Elias Stays
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Offered a London post, Elias declines. He learns to read her lips, her hands, her written verses. Their love rebuilds on new ground, quieter and more deliberate. Beat: love against duty resolved — both kept, neither sacrificed wholly.

chapters.title: The Last Patient
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Years later, an old man in the hospice counts backwards; when he reaches one, a distant bell tolls once, warm as lamplight, and his face eases. Rosalind whispers the only words left to her: 'You're home.' Beat: grace earned; the horror transmuted into mercy.

chapters.title: Old Chapel Road, Late
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Rosalind's POV, years on. She walks the road at dusk on solstice eve, touches the garden wall where the chapel stood, and listens to the small bell waiting inside her chest. The lights are on. The doors are counted. Beat: closure — vigilance as love, the story ringing softly onward.
